title: About
text:
I am a die hard sports fan. I watch a wide variety of sports from F1 to the American Cornhole League to your casual NFL Sundays.
I am originally from Baton Rouge, LA. So I do bleed purple and gold and believes no body can beat the Saints. These two teams, and my entire family, were driving factories in my decision to become a member of sports media.
These are some of my sports takes and findings, with all of the graphs and charts to show you where I am right and wrong.

title: Is the SEC or BIG10 the True Power Conference
text:
Is the Big10 truly taking over the SEC’s spot as the best conference?
Let’s look at last year’s stats to figure that out. I will be using the 2024 football logs from mattwaite.github.io.
The first stats that I want to take a look at is on the offensive side of the ball. While defense does win championships, you need to score to win. I am going to be looking at each SEC and Big 10’s rushing and passing game from last year.


Code
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)

football <- read_csv("https://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/footballlogs24.csv")

ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


Code
BOff <- football |> 
  group_by(Conference, Team) |> 
  summarise(
    RushingYards = sum(RushingYds),
    PassingYards = sum(PassingYds))|>
  mutate(
    Yards=RushingYards + PassingYards
  ) |> 
  filter(Conference %in% c("Big Ten Conference", "Southeastern Conference"))


`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Conference'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.


Code
SOff <- BOff |> 
  filter(Conference %in% c("Southeastern Conference"))

ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(data=BOff, aes(x=reorder(Team, Yards), weight=Yards)) +
  geom_bar(data=SOff, aes(x=reorder(Team, Yards), weight=Yards, fill ="red")) +
  coord_flip() +
labs(
    y = "Total Offensive Yards",
    x = "Team",
    title = "10 of the top 15 offenses are in the SEC",
    subtitle = "The SEC shows more depth when it comes to offense",
     caption="Source: mattwaite.github.io | By: JAGGER HOPKINS"
  ) + 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

Seeing that the SEC shows more depth when it comes to offense. Let’s take a look at their respective defenses. Like stated before defense wins championships, and the SEC has been known for having outstanding defense year in and year out. In this graph I will be showing you the defensive stats that are the most important to me. Limiting first downs is the foundation to a good defense, if they can’t get a first down, they cant move the ball. The other two stats are a little bit more obvious, who gets more takeaways and who limits touchdowns. Obviously you need to limit touchdowns, that is the entire point of the defense going on the field.If the defense can get takeaways and create opportunities for the offense, that’s when a defense beccomes lethal.

In this last graph I will be combined offense and defense. See how these two sides of the field come together and show us what’s what. I will be looking at the team total wins, and their defensive and offensive yards per play. See which teams are being productive both offensively and defensively, who’s limiting offense and who’s torching the defense.


Code
library(ggrepel)
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
OD <- read_csv("https://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/footballlogs24.csv")


Rows: 1711 Columns: 54
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr   (8): HomeAway, Opponent, Result, TeamFull, TeamURL, Outcome, Team, Con...
dbl  (45): Game, PassingCmp, PassingAtt, PassingPct, PassingYds, PassingTD, ...
date  (1): Date

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


Code
winlosslogs <- OD |> 
  mutate(
    wins = case_when(
      grepl("W", Outcome) ~ 1, 
      grepl("L", Outcome) ~ 0)
)
ypp <- winlosslogs |> 
  group_by(Team, Conference) |> 
  summarise(
    TotalPlays = sum(OffensivePlays), 
    TotalYards = sum(OffensiveYards), 
    DefensivePlays = sum(DefPlays), 
    DefensiveYards = sum(DefYards), 
    TotalWins = sum(wins)) |>
  filter(Conference %in% c("Big Ten Conference", "Southeastern Conference")) |>
  mutate(
    OffensiveYPP = TotalYards/TotalPlays, 
    DefensiveYPP = DefensiveYards/DefensivePlays)


`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Team'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.


Code
bigten <- ypp |>
  filter(Conference =="Big Ten Conference")
sec <- ypp |>
  filter(Conference =="Southeastern Conference")

ypp |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  summarise(
    offense = mean(OffensiveYPP), 
    defense = mean(DefensiveYPP)
    )

title: New Orleans Saints’ Empty Throne
text:
The New Orleans Saints have been in nothing but decline after the retirement of one of the greatest to ever do it, Drew Brees. Brees was retiring after a pretty successful season, leading the NFC south with a 12-4 record and ultimately losing to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the divisional round of the playoffs.
Even with Sean Payton staying for the 2021 season, there was still confusion as to who should replace Brees and lead the franchise to more success. Since Brees retired the Saints have had 7 different quarterbacks to start one or more games.
While there were options, they were not of the highest caliber.There were questions about Jamies Winston coming into the regular season, yes he sat behind Brees for a season but he just got off of a 30-30 season. Yes the infamous 30 touchdowns and 30 interceptions season.
The next best option was Taysom Hill, the football swiss army knife. There was promise, he put the NFL on notice by doing everything on the field while being able to throw darts. Sean Payton knew that Hill could step in for the staring job, but did Payton want to give up such a versatile athlete by making him the start. To keep it simple, no.
Since this dilemma the Saints have had 7 different quarterbacks to start one or more games.
In the past two season the Saints have combined for a total of 12 wins, the total Brees had in his final season. The season that everyone called Brees washed. So to say that New Orleans has been in turmoil is an understatement.
The first question I want to ask is, who is scoring while limiting turnovers. Here are the 7 quarterbacks, notice that * means combined seasons.

Since 2020 Derek Carr leads the saints in single season touchdowns with 25, leading Brees by one. The next best being Andy Dalton with 18, every other quarterback having 11 or less passing touchdowns.
Touchdowns and Interceptions are very important to a quarterback and his offense, but its not everything. A good quarterback should be able to accurately push the ball down the field. This plays off touchdowns and interceptions, in a way. If a quarterback is scoring a lot of touchdowns and minimizing interceptions, then one should notice a good completion percentage and yards per attempt.
How does the theory apply to the Saints quarterbackss?

Since the Saints have had a lot of different quarterbacks, lets take a look a just the season. After all it is a team sport.
One of the most talked about attributes talked about when talking about productive quarterbacks is decision making. Is he making the right read, or does he look panic and rushing the throw the ball. There have been three different rookies that have started for the Saints, so you would expect there to be some bad balls thrown.
So lets take a look at the Saints bad throw and on target throw percentage since 2020.

title: No Need to Change Laundry: Bellevue West QB Will Anderson Commits to UNI
text:
Will Anderson is a talented quarterback standing at 6’1” in the 2026 class, hailing from Omaha, NE. He has been the starting quarterback for Bellevue West High School for the past two years. He is set to join the University of Northern Iowa as the sole quarterback signing with the Panthers for the December 2025 signing period.
“It was pretty exciting,” said Senior quarterback Will Anderson. “I was ready to get the whole process done with and officially become a Panther. But it was exciting to see all my friends, parents, and family there, all watching me sign. I couldn’t get my hand to stop shaking during my speech; I just kept shaking. But yeah, it was a fun and really surreal moment that I’ll never forget.”
Anderson started at Millard West, earning split starts while demonstrating his playmaking ability. He transferred to Bellevue West in his sophomore year, developing behind senior quarterback Daniel Kaelin. Injuries, including a non-throwing arm labrum, plagued his junior season. As he approached his senior season and led his team into the playoffs, tragedy struck again when he suffered a grade 3 MCL tear, which he has since recovered to grade 1.
“Right away, I kind of knew right away, I knew it was pretty bad,” Senior quarterback Will Andersen. “Didn’t know where, or who, what the injury was, but I heard a pop and knew something with my knee. So right away, on the sidelines, I knew I was probably done for the year, which is pretty emotional.”
Starting his career, Anderson came to Millard West mentally preparing himself to get on the field and stay on it. Anderson knew he would have to earn the upperclassmen’s trust and respect if he was to play varsity as a freshman.
Anderson did precisely that, earning split reps on the varsity squad as a freshman in week one against Millard South. In that game, Anderson showed everyone exactly what he knew he was capable of, ending his first career drive with a 69-yard touchdown pass to then junior wide receiver Jackson Williams.
“Coach Long from Millard West and Jackson Williams, too, really just took me under their wing and tried to develop me as well,” Anderson said. “Even Jackson Williams, as a receiver, helped me a lot on the field by calming me down. In the huddle, if I was too amped up, or if I would miss a throw from being too anxious, he’d calm me down, get the nerves down, and get me in a flow state.”
While Williams was someone to lean on in the game, his mother, Stephanie Anderson, was with him and supported him throughout his entire career. Anderson would make sure to look up to his mother in the stands after every touchdown that he got.
Stephanie would turn out to be more than just a supporter but also another football mind at home for Anderson, as she would tell him what he should be looking for in coaches and what offenses he would work best in. While she wasn’t on the field, Stephanie was still feeling the same emotions.
“It was the first game of the year when they played Millard West,” Stephanie Anderson said. “I was so nervous I felt like I couldn’t breathe. That snap, he got the ball, and he was in, I actually think he ran over a coach on the sideline. But he was pushing the ball down the field. Then he threw a beautiful pass that resulted in a TD. The crowd went wild. I knew then Will was doing what he loved.”

After his freshman season, Anderson transferred to his current high school, Bellevue West, where he sat behind Daniel Kaelin. Kaelin would be a great player to sit behind and learn from, as he would ultimately flip his commitment from Missouri to Nebraska and transfer to his current spot at Virginia.
Kaelin would be crucial in Anderson’s development in the Bellevue West program and as a player. Kaelin would be the medium between the coaches’ knowledge and actually seeing and learning what they are saying. Anderson would spend the season taking bits and pieces from Kaelin’s game and adding them to his own.
Anderson still got to see the field in nine games throughout the year. Taking those opportunities and proving himself was all that was on his mind. Anderson ended his sophomore year with nine touchdowns on the ground and in the air, with the longest being from 90 yards out.
“I think what Danny(Daniel Kaelin) did a really good job,” Bellevue West Head coach Mike Huffman stated. “We coach the kids, we show them things, but at the end of the day, we’re old people who haven’t played in a long time. So when you hear something from a coach, and then you have a peer who’s actually in the battle doing it, it can give little nuances. And the beauty was, you saw Will doing that this year to our younger quarterbacks. So, it was really a cool deal, kind of giving back what was given to him. Danny was an exceptional leader and a student of the game. And I think that showed Will, at a really, really early age, what it takes to be a successful high-school quarterback and a quarterback that has an opportunity to play in college.”

Junior year was all about grit and toughness from Anderson. During the season, Anderson suffered multiple injuries, including him tearing his left labrum, which resulted in him missing a game. Anderson would not get surgery until after his senior season, but coach Huffman would be wary of his shoulder and limit his running. This season, however, would be the second time in Anderon’s career that he has taken snaps in the playoffs.
Anderson ended his junior campaign with 10 starts, 1865 passing yards, 21 touchdowns and a career high in rushing yards with 252.
“I think it (junior season) was very important, but honestly, I was pretty underwhelmed with how it went,” Anderson said. “I feel like I could have played better, and feel like I should have toughened a few things out, and feel like I missed too many quarters or minutes with injuries. I was pretty banged up the whole season, which is pretty painful looking back at it, but I mean, I showed a glimpse of what I could do, and my stats weren’t what I wanted, but I had a good highlight tape, which really helped me go far in recruiting.”
Entering his senior season with seven Division II offers and a Division I offer from the University of Northern Iowa.
Before tearing his MCL in the last regular season game, Anderson ended with a career high in touchdowns and passing yards with 2,041 yards and 25 touchdowns. Anderson officially signed to UNI on Wednesday, Dec. 3, 2025.
“Just want to try and get a shot or chance to play early,” Anderson stated. ” I feel like I can, but I need to get in the playbook and get up there, start practicing with all the guys and really prove that I belong there.
